questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: The primary structure of a protein refers to _____.

options.text: Linear structure and order of the amino acids present
Regular conformational forms of a protein
Complete three dimensional structure of the polypeptide units of a given protein

questions.correctAnswerText: Linear structure and order of the amino acids present
questions.explanation: The primary structure of a protein refers to the linear structure and order of the amino acids present. There are four known levels of protein structure: Primary — a linear sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain; Secondary — folded and geometrically ordered units of short segments of polypeptides, e.g. alpha helix, beta-pleated sheets, loops, and bends; Tertiary — secondary structures arranged into larger functional units; Quaternary — different types of polypeptides arranged in a spatial manner.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding alpha helix?

options.text: Stability of an alpha helix arises primarily from the peptide bond.
A complete turn of an alpha helix contains 3.6 amino acyl residues.
Pitch of the helix is 0.54 nm.
Large numbers of charged amino acids disrupt the helix.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stability of an alpha helix arises primarily from the peptide bond.
questions.explanation: Alpha helix is stabilized primarily by intra-chain hydrogen bonds. Alpha helix is the most common and stable secondary structure of protein. It is a rigid, right-handed spiral. A complete turn contains an average of 3.6 aminoacyl residues and the rise per turn (pitch) is 0.54 nm. Large numbers of charged amino acids (glutamate, aspartate, histidine, lysine, and arginine) disrupt the helix by forming ionic bonds or by electrostatically repelling each other.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: What is the most common and stable conformation for a polypeptide chain?
questions.explanation: The most common and stable conformation for a polypeptide chain is alpha helix. Hemoglobin and myoglobin are proteins whose major secondary structure is the alpha helix.

questions.question: Which of the following amino acids do not participate in the formation of an alpha helix?
questions.explanation: Proline does not participate in the formation of an alpha helix. Stability of an alpha helix arises primarily from hydrogen bonds between the peptide-bond carbonyl oxygen and the peptide-bond nitrogen hydrogen of the fourth residue down the chain. Since the peptide-bond nitrogen of proline lacks a hydrogen atom, it cannot form this hydrogen bond.

questions.question: Which among the following is true about denaturation of proteins?

options.text: Biological property of the protein is retained.
It mostly renders the protein insoluble.

questions.explanation: Denaturation mostly renders the protein insoluble. Protein denaturation causes unfolding and disorganization of secondary and tertiary structures, so biological properties are lost. Peptide bonds forming the primary structure are not hydrolyzed. questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: What do chaperones assist in?
questions.explanation: Chaperones assist in protein folding. Chaperones are heat-shock proteins that bind short hydrophobic sequences of an extended polypeptide, shielding a newly synthesized chain from aggregation and allowing appropriate secondary structure to form. Chaperones can also rescue proteins trapped in misfolded dead-end forms, giving them another chance to fold productively.

Derived proteins are degradation products of native proteins.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: An infant is brought to the pediatric OPD with clinical findings as shown in the image. Further examination shows that the child has a loss of developmental milestones, truncal hypotonia, and failure to thrive. Which of the following enzymes is defective in this child?
questions.explanation: The image shows an infant with sparse and kinky hair; together with loss of developmental milestones and truncal hypotonia this suggests Menkes disease, caused by defective lysyl oxidase. Menkes disease results from deficiency of the lysyl-oxidase cofactor copper due to an ATP7A defect that prevents intestinal copper absorption. ATP7A mutation causes Menkes disease (X-linked recessive); ATP7B mutation causes Wilson disease (autosomal recessive).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following types of collagens is involved in wound healing?
questions.explanation: Type III collagen is involved in wound healing. Types I and III predominate in skin and aponeurotic layers. In early healing, type III collagen is synthesized and is later replaced by type I. Tensile strength is related to amount/type of collagen and collagen cross-links; approximately 80% of original tissue strength is obtained by six weeks after surgery, and wounds may never regain 100% of previous strength.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is caused by the lack of a specific lysosomal hydrolase for glycoproteins?
questions.explanation: Lack of a specific lysosomal hydrolase for glycoproteins causes glycoprotein storage diseases (oligosaccharidoses), a group of rare autosomal recessive diseases. Lysosomal acid hydrolases sequentially remove oligosaccharide groups in reverse order of incorporation. Deficiency of one hydrolase causes accumulation of partially degraded glycoproteins in lysosomes.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following disease is associated with defective glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI)?
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria results from defective glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI). GPI is required to attach decay-accelerating factor (DAF/CD55) and CD59 to the RBC membrane. Loss of these proteins allows complement-mediated RBC hemolysis. Symptoms listed include anemia, esophageal spasm, erectile dysfunction, abdominal pain and pulmonary hypertension. Treatment is eculizumab, a terminal complement inhibitor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following features will not be seen in a patient with I-cell disease?
questions.explanation: Buphthalmos is not a feature of I-cell disease. I-cell disease is an inherited lysosomal storage disorder caused by a defect in Golgi N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, causing failure to phosphorylate mannose residues (mannose-6-phosphate) on glycoproteins. Proteins are secreted extracellularly rather than delivered to lysosomes, which lack normal enzymes and accumulate inclusion bodies. Features listed include coarse facial features, gingival hyperplasia, clouded corneas, restricted joint movement, claw-hand deformity, kyphoscoliosis and high plasma lysosomal enzymes.

questions.question: Which of the following would have no effect on the function of the protein product?
questions.explanation: When glutamine is replaced by asparagine, there is no change in protein-product function. This is a conservative or homologous amino-acid replacement because asparagine and glutamine are both uncharged polar (hydrophilic) amino acids, preserving polarity and charge.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: What is the function of the proteasome?
questions.explanation: The proteasome takes part in protein degradation. It is a cylindrical cytosolic structure that degrades polyubiquitinated proteins, with a central core containing proteolytic enzymes and regulatory rings that admit ubiquitin-tagged proteins. It also contributes to antigen presentation to T lymphocytes by degrading viruses and other molecules into small peptides.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.question: Which of the following is true about the structural organization of proteins?

options.text: Primary, secondary and tertiary structures are destroyed by denaturation
Secondary structure is stabilised by disulphide bonds
Secondary and tertiary structures depend upon amino acid sequence

questions.explanation: Tertiary structure is three-dimensional. Protein organization is described as primary (linear amino-acid sequence), secondary (folded geometrically ordered short segments such as alpha helix, beta sheets, loops and bends), tertiary (secondary structures arranged into larger functional domains), and quaternary (different polypeptides arranged spatially). Denaturation disrupts secondary and tertiary structures without hydrolyzing primary peptide bonds. Hydrogen bonds and van der Waals interactions stabilize secondary structure, whereas disulfide bonds stabilize tertiary structure. The source states that primary structure depends on amino-acid sequence.
